title: Checking if Two Binary Trees Are Identical

phrases.explanation: Having the exact same shape and arrangement of nodes
The simplest condition in a recursive function that stops further recursion
Visit every node in the tree following a specific order
An unusual or extreme input that tests the boundaries of a solution
Processing nodes one depth at a time, from top to bottom

technical_terms.definition: A tree data structure where each node has at most two children, called left and right
A technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller subproblems
Breadth-First Search, an algorithm that explores nodes level by level using a queue
Depth-First Search, an algorithm that explores as deep as possible before backtracking
A first-in-first-out data structure used in breadth-first traversal

java_methods.description: Creates a new queue backed by a linked list, commonly used for BFS
Adds a node to the end of the queue

concept: Given two binary trees, determine if they are structurally identical with the same node values. Two trees are considered the same if they have the same structure and every corresponding node has the same value.

solutions.label: Recursive DFS
solutions.summary: Recursively compare each corresponding node in both trees. If both nodes are null, they match. If one is null or values differ, they don't match. Otherwise, recurse on left and right children.

solutions.label: Iterative BFS with Queue
solutions.summary: Use a queue to compare nodes level by level. Push pairs of corresponding nodes and check each pair for equality as you dequeue them.

sections.diagram:

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's your problem. You're given the roots of two binary trees, p and q. Write a function that returns true if the two trees are identical, meaning they have the same structure and the same values at every node.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So I need to compare both shape and values. A few clarifying questions: can the trees be empty? And what type are the node values?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, either or both trees can be empty, meaning the root is null. Node values are integers. The number of nodes ranges from zero to one hundred.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What about duplicates? Can the same value appear more than once in a tree?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, duplicates are allowed. The key point is that every corresponding position must have the same value.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So if both roots are null, return true. If only one is null, return false. Otherwise, check that values match and both subtrees are identical. Let me walk through some approaches.

sections.title: Recursive DFS
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    S["isSameTree p=1, q=1"]:::blue --> L["isSameTree p=2, q=2"]:::blue
    S --> R["isSameTree p=3, q=3"]:::blue
    L --> LL["isSameTree null, null → true"]:::blue
    L --> LR["isSameTree null, null → true"]:::blue
    R --> RL["isSameTree null, null → true"]:::blue
    R --> RR["isSameTree null, null → true"]:::blue
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is a recursive approach using depth-first search. The base cases are straightforward: if both nodes are null, return true. If only one is null, or the values differ, return false.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Then I recursively call the function on the left children of both trees and the right children of both trees. Only if both calls return true do we return true.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through an example. Say both trees are: root one, left child two, right child three.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: We start at the roots. Both are one, so values match. We recurse left: both are two, values match. Then we recurse on their children, which are all null, so we return true. Same on the right with three. Everything matches, so the result is true.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time and space complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time complexity is O of n, where n is the smaller number of nodes, since we visit each node once. Space complexity is O of h, where h is the tree height, due to the recursion stack. In the worst case of a skewed tree, that becomes O of n.

sections.title: Iterative BFS with Queue
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    Q0["Queue: pair 1,1"]:::purple --> CHECK1["Dequeue: 1==1 ✓"]:::purple
    CHECK1 --> Q1["Queue: pair 2,2 | pair 3,3"]:::purple
    Q1 --> CHECK2["Dequeue: 2==2 ✓"]:::purple
    CHECK2 --> Q2["Queue: pair 3,3"]:::purple
    Q2 --> CHECK3["Dequeue: 3==3 ✓"]:::purple
    CHECK3 --> DONE["Queue empty → true"]:::purple
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: An alternative is an iterative approach using breadth-first search. I use a queue that stores pairs of nodes, one from each tree. I start by adding both roots as a pair.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For each pair I dequeue, if both are null I continue. If only one is null or values differ, I return false. Otherwise, I enqueue the left children as a pair and the right children as a pair.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Use the same example: root one, left two, right three for both trees.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I enqueue the pair one and one. I dequeue it, values match, then enqueue pairs two-two and three-three. I dequeue two-two, values match, their children are null so nothing is added. I dequeue three-three, same thing. The queue is empty, so I return true.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How does this compare to the recursive approach in complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is still O of n. Space is O of n in the worst case because the queue can hold up to an entire level of the tree. For a balanced tree, the widest level has about n over two nodes. The advantage is we avoid recursion stack overflow on very deep trees.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good work. Which approach would you recommend in an interview?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I'd go with the recursive DFS approach. It's clean, easy to explain, and has better space complexity for balanced trees. The iterative BFS is worth mentioning as a follow-up since it avoids stack overflow on extremely deep trees.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Agreed. The recursive solution is elegant and shows strong understanding of tree traversal. Both are valid and run in linear time.
